    Summary and Schedule

    Introduction to Computing is a six-week beginner course from the Australian Data and Cyber Institute (ADCI). It explains how computers work, how they store and move data, and how computing affects people and society. It prepares you for the computing units in a Bachelor of Cyber Security or a Bachelor of Data Science.

    It is for complete beginners, especially working adults who want to move into cyber security, data or computing. You do not need any technical background. Each week takes 6 hours or less.

    You do not need to install anything. Everything runs in your web browser, so the course works on a locked-down work laptop. There is no programming language in this course. Python is taught in the separate Introduction to Programming course.

    Learning outcomes

    By the end of the six weeks you will be able to:

    • LO 1 Explain how a computer turns data into information and how its hardware parts work together, with a brief view of how computers got here.
    • LO 2 Represent data in binary and hexadecimal, explain how numbers, text, images and files are stored, and apply basic logic.
    • LO 3 Tell system software from application software, and use an operating system, including its command line, to manage files.
    • LO 4 Solve a problem with an algorithm, written as pseudocode and a flowchart, using sequence, selection and repetition.
    • LO 5 Explain how networks, the internet and the cloud work, and apply security, privacy and ethical principles to computing.

    How each week works

    Each week is one episode in the menu. Open a week to see its parts: the week overview, the sections (such as 1.1 and 1.2), the Concepts Bridge and the practice task. Every week follows the same blocks:

    Block Time What you do
    Watch about 0.5 to 1 h Short videos listed on the week overview
    Read & practise about 1 to 2 h The week’s sections: read, try each tool, do the exercises
    Concepts Bridge 30 min One idea that links the week to cyber security or data science
    Build 2 h (3 h in Week 6) Your portfolio item: a practice task with a worksheet
    Quiz 15 min A short quiz in Canvas, marked automatically

    Your portfolio for each week is submitted at the end of the week and marked by your tutor.

    Prerequisite

    Prerequisites

    • No technical experience is needed.
    • A computer with an up-to-date web browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari) and an internet connection.
    • Read the Setup page before Week 1.
    Setup Instructions Download files required for the lesson
    Duration: 00h 00m  1. Week 1: Computer fundamentals, a brief history, and hardware What will I learn in Week 1, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    What does a computer actually do?
    How did computers get from room-sized machines to phones?
    What are the main parts inside a computer, and what does each one do?
    How can every computer be described in the same four steps?
    Can I describe the computer I use every day?
    Duration: 05h 10m  2. Week 2: Data representation and logic What will I learn in Week 2, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    Why do computers use binary?
    How do I convert between decimal, binary and hexadecimal?
    How are text, colours and whole files stored as numbers?
    How can simple on-off switches make decisions and add numbers?
    Why does a 1 TB drive show less than 1,000 GB?
    Can I read data the way a computer stores it?
    Duration: 10h 25m  3. Week 3: Software and operating systems What will I learn in Week 3, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    What is the difference between application software and system software?
    What does an operating system do?
    How are files and folders organised?
    How do I control a computer by typing commands?
    Why should people only have the access they need?
    Can I audit software and use the command line on a real log?
    Duration: 15h 35m  4. Week 4: Algorithms and programming basics What will I learn in Week 4, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    What is an algorithm, and how do I design one?
    What are the building blocks every program uses?
    How do searching algorithms compare?
    How does a CPU run a program, one instruction at a time?
    How does a program in a language like Python reach the CPU?
    Can I design and test an algorithm before any code is written?
    Duration: 20h 50m  5. Week 5: Networks, the internet and online safety What will I learn in Week 5, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    How does data travel across networks and the internet?
    What happens between my browser and a web server?
    What are the common online threats, and how do I protect against them?
    What happens, step by step, when I open a web page?
    Can I investigate how real websites are found, reached and secured?
    Duration: 02h 05m  6. Week 6: Data, the cloud, ethics and society What will I learn in Week 6, and how should I spend my 6 hours?
    What kinds of data are there, and how should they be looked after?
    What is the cloud, and what are its benefits and risks?
    What protects people’s data in Australia?
    How does computing affect society?
    Who collects data about me in an ordinary day, and what rules apply?
    Can I bring the whole course together to advise a real-world business?
    Duration: 07h 15m Finish

    The actual schedule may vary slightly depending on the topics and exercises chosen by the instructor.

    You do not need to install anything. Every tool in this course runs in a web browser, and none of them needs an account. This page is a short checklist so that you are ready for Week 1.

    What you need

    Discussion

    Before Week 1

    • A computer with an up-to-date web browser: Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari. A work laptop is fine.
    • A reliable internet connection that can play YouTube videos.
    • A way to write and save your work: any text editor, Word or Google Docs. You submit each week’s portfolio as a Markdown (.md), Word or PDF file.
    • A way to take a screenshot: Windows key + Shift + S on Windows, or Cmd + Shift + 4 on a Mac.

    The free browser tools you will use

    Week Tool What it is for
    2 HexEd.it Looking at the bytes inside a file. Files are opened in your browser, not uploaded.
    2 CircuitVerse Building logic circuits. Use it as a guest.
    3 JSLinux A real Linux system running inside your browser
    4 diagrams.net Drawing flowcharts and diagrams
    4 Little Man Computer A simple simulated CPU
    5 Your browser’s developer tools and certificate viewer Seeing requests, status codes and certificates
    5 Google Admin Toolbox Dig Looking up DNS records
    5 Google Phishing Quiz Practising spotting phishing emails. Use a made-up name and email.
    5 CyberChef Trying encoding and hashing
    5 httpstatus.io Checking status codes if developer tools are blocked
    Callout

    On a work laptop

    Your employer’s IT team may block some tools or settings. That is fine:

    • Each task says what to do if a tool is blocked, and you will not be marked down.
    • If there is no fallback, try a home or library computer, and tell your tutor.

    Course files

    Some practice tasks use files, such as worksheets, a server log and three “mystery” files. Each task links to the files it needs, or you can download them all at once in the course files zip. Unzip it into a folder you can find again.

    Privacy in this course

    You will never be asked for personal details. Do not record your computer’s serial number, device name, user name or IP address, or any passwords, in your work. All the businesses and people in the case studies are invented.
